entities.summary:
The Green Party (various national iterations), originating in the Values Party of New Zealand (1972) and the German Die Grünen (1980), pioneered the integration of environmentalism, feminism, and post-materialism into mainstream electoral politics. The German Greens' 1983 entry into the Bundestag (with 5.6%) was the first successful entry of an environmental party into a major European parliament, establishing a template adopted worldwide. The Greens became governing coalition partners in Germany (1998-2005, 2021-), gaining a cabinet minister position for the first time.

The Values Party of New Zealand (1972) was the world's first national-level environmental party. German Die Grünen was founded in 1980 from the anti-nuclear, feminist, and peace movements of 1970s West Germany — refusing traditional parliamentary norms with principles of decentralization, grassroots democracy, and rotation of seats. Rudolf Bahro, Petra Kelly, and Joschka Fischer were founding figures. The Greens' 1983 Bundestag entry — with members arriving at the Reichstag carrying tree saplings — represented post-materialism entering German politics.

Joschka Fischer's 1998-2005 role as Germany's Foreign Minister in the SPD-Green coalition was the first time a former street activist led a European country's foreign policy. Fischer's support for NATO's Kosovo intervention (1999) — against Green pacifism — created the defining intra-Green ideological tension. By 2021, Greens participated in governments across Germany (federal and 11 states), Austria, Finland, and Ireland, demonstrating environmental parties' governing maturity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The German Greens' 1983 Bundestag entry — and subsequent governing coalitions — established the template for environmental parties worldwide, transforming environmentalism from a protest movement into a governing political force now in coalitions across Europe.
